conversation.content: Design a social media feed like Twitter. Users post tweets, follow others, and see a chronological feed. I expect depth on the trade-offs. Where do you start?
I'd want to know the scale. How many users, how many tweets per day, and how quickly the feed needs to load.
500M DAU, 500M tweets per day, feed loads in under 200ms. Some users have 50M+ followers. What's your high-level approach?

The main challenge is generating the feed. When a user opens the app, we need to show the latest tweets from people they follow. Two approaches: fan-out-on-write — when someone tweets, push it to all followers' feeds immediately. Or fan-out-on-read — when a user opens the app, pull the latest tweets from everyone they follow and merge. I'd go with fan-out-on-write because reads are way more frequent than writes, and we want reads to be fast.
You mentioned users with 50M followers. If that user tweets, fan-out-on-write means writing to 50 million feed timelines. What's the implication?

That's a lot of writes. It would take a long time — maybe minutes — to fan out to 50M feeds. And during that time, some followers see the tweet and others don't. So for celebrities, maybe we do fan-out-on-read instead? A hybrid approach — fan-out-on-write for regular users and fan-out-on-read for celebrities.
Good. What's the threshold for celebrity treatment? And what does the hybrid read path look like?

Maybe anyone with over 10,000 followers is treated as a celebrity. On read, the user's pre-built feed (from normal users via fan-out-on-write) is fetched from cache. Then we also fetch the latest tweets from celebrity accounts the user follows and merge them in. The merge happens at read time, sorted by timestamp. The number of celebrity accounts a user follows is probably small — maybe 20-50 — so fetching their latest tweets is manageable.
Where do you store the pre-built feeds? And how much memory does that require?

Redis. Each user has a list of tweet IDs in Redis, sorted by time. For 500M users... that's a lot. If each feed stores 500 tweet IDs at 8 bytes each, that's 4KB per user, times 500M users = 2TB. That's big but feasible with a Redis cluster — maybe 20 machines with 128GB each.
Do you actually need feeds for all 500M users? Many might not log in regularly.

Good point. We could only maintain feeds for active users — those who've logged in within the last, say, 7 days. That might cut the number in half. When an inactive user returns, we build their feed on-demand using fan-out-on-read, then start maintaining it going forward.
Now, at staff level, I'd expect you to go beyond chronological ordering. How would you rank the feed?

Algorithmic ranking... we could score each tweet based on engagement signals — likes, retweets, replies — and the user's past interactions with the author. Tweets from accounts the user interacts with frequently would rank higher. The scoring could be a simple weighted formula or an ML model trained on engagement data. I'm less familiar with the specifics of how ranking models work at scale though.
At staff level, the ranking system is one of the most complex and impactful components. Can you go deeper on the ML pipeline?

Right, so the ML pipeline would... collect features for each tweet-user pair: author features (follower count, post frequency), tweet features (age, engagement rate, media type), and user features (interest categories, interaction history). These feed into a model that predicts engagement probability — P(click), P(like), P(retweet). The final score combines these probabilities, weighted by business objectives. I know this at a high level but I'd struggle with the implementation details — the feature store, model serving at 500M DAU, and the A/B testing framework.
What about trending topics? How does that work?

Count hashtag and keyword frequency over a sliding time window. If a topic's mention rate is significantly above its baseline, it's trending. We could use a streaming system — Kafka plus a stream processor — that counts mentions per minute and compares against the moving average. The tricky part is excluding spam and manipulation — coordinated bot campaigns inflating a topic. I'd apply some velocity-based filtering: a topic that goes from 0 to 100K mentions in 1 minute is likely artificial; a gradual ramp-up from news coverage is more likely organic.
What happens if the Redis feed cache goes down? Millions of users can't load their feed.

We'd fall back to fan-out-on-read for everyone — query the database for the latest tweets from followed accounts. It's slower but functional. The database would need to handle the sudden spike — we should have read replicas sized for this scenario. And we should run Redis as a cluster with replication so a single node failure doesn't take out the whole cache.
We're out of time. Any final thoughts?

Search with Elasticsearch for full-text tweet search. Notifications pipeline for mentions and likes. And content moderation — detecting hate speech and misinformation, which is probably one of the hardest problems on the platform.
Thanks. You showed solid understanding of the feed fanout model, but the depth on ranking ML and failure handling didn't quite meet staff expectations.

strengths: Good hybrid fanout design with celebrity threshold and merge-on-read
Solid memory estimation for Redis feed storage with practical optimization (active users only)
Decent trending topic design with spam velocity filtering
weaknesses: Ranking ML discussion was surface-level — acknowledged the gap but couldn't go deeper. Staff should have stronger ML system knowledge
Failure handling was thin — didn't discuss graceful degradation, circuit breakers, or cache warming strategies
No discussion of Snowflake IDs, data partitioning strategy, or social graph storage
Content moderation mentioned as a bullet point without design depth — at staff level should discuss the ML pipeline
Requirements gathering was minimal — didn't drive the conversation as expected at staff level
